You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

# `PIXterm` - *draw images in your ANSI terminal with true color*

**`PIXterm`** ***shows images directly in your terminal***, recreating the pixels through a combination of [ANSI character background color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code#Colors) and the [unicode lower half block element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_Elements). If image has transparency, an optional matte color can be used for background. Also, you can specify a dithering mode; in which case, the image is rendered using block elements with different shades, or using standard ASCII characters in the same way. In dithering mode, the matte color is used to fill the background of the blocks or characters.

Supported image formats: JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF, WebP.

Fetching images from HTTP/HTTPS is supported too.

## Usage

```
pixterm [options] <image file or URL>
```

### Options

- `-version` - show PIXterm version
- `-credits` - show some love to contributors <3
- `-d <mode>` - dithering mode:
  - `0` - no dithering (default)
  - `1` - with blocks
  - `2` - with chars
- `-go` - output Go code to 'fmt.Print()' the image
- `-m <color>` - matte color for transparency or background (optional, hex format, default: 000000)
- `-nobg` - disable background color (optional, only in dithering mode, ignores matte color)
- `-s <method>` - scale method:
  - `0` - resize (default)
  - `1` - fill
  - `2` - fit
- `-tr <rows>` - terminal rows (optional, >=2; when piping, default: 24)
- `-tc <columns>` - terminal columns (optional, >=2; when piping, default: 80)

## Requirements

Your terminal emulator must support *true color* in order to display image colors correctly. In addition, you must use a monospaced font that includes the lower half block unicode character: `▄ (U+2584)`. [Envy Code R](https://damieng.com/blog/2008/05/26/envy-code-r-preview-7-coding-font-released) is recommended. If you want to use the dithering mode with blocks, the font must also include the following unicode characters: `█ (U+2588)`, `▓ (U+2593)`, `▒ (U+2592)`, `░ (U+2591)`. The dithering mode with characters works with standard ASCII chars.

def run_with_pty_size(args, rows, cols, img="/tmp/test2x2.png"):
    master, slave = pty.openpty()
    # Set winsize: struct winsize {ws_row, ws_col, ws_xpixel, ws_ypixel} (4 shorts, HHHH)
    winsize = struct.pack("HHHH", rows, cols, 0, 0)
    fcntl.ioctl(slave, termios.TIOCSWINSZ, winsize)

            if not data:
                break
            output+=data
        except OSError:
            break

    err=proc.stderr.read()

# Craft minimal 2x2 24-bit BMP (uncompressed, BITMAPINFOHEADER, bottom-up, BGR, padded to 4-byte rows)
# BMP file: 14-byte BITMAPFILEHEADER + 40-byte BITMAPINFOHEADER + pixel data
# For 2x2 24-bit: each row has 2 pixels *3 bytes =6 bytes, padded to 8 bytes (multiple of 4) with 2 padding bytes per row. Total pixel data =8*2=16 bytes. File size =14+40+16=70 bytes.
import struct

def make_bmp_2x2(pixels_top_to_bottom):
    # pixels_top_to_bottom: list of 2 rows, each row list of 2 (R,G,B) tuples, top row first
    # BMP stores bottom-up: bottom row first
    # Each pixel BGR (B,G,R)
    # Each row padded to 4-byte boundary
    width, height = 2, 2
    # BITMAPFILEHEADER (14 bytes): bfType(2)=BM(0x4D42), bfSize(4), bfReserved1(2)=0, bfReserved2(2)=0, bfOffBits(4)=54 (14+40)
    bfType = 0x4D42
    bfOffBits = 14+40
    # Row size padded: ((width*3 +3)//4)*4 = ((6+3)//4)*4= (9//4)*4=2*4=8
    row_padded = ((width*3+3)//4)*4
    pixel_data_size = row_padded*height
    bfSize = bfOffBits + pixel_data_size
    file_header = struct.pack('<HIHHI', bfType, bfSize, 0, 0, bfOffBits)
    # BITMAPINFOHEADER (40 bytes): biSize(4)=40, biWidth(4)=2, biHeight(4)=2 (positive=bottom-up), biPlanes(2)=1, biBitCount(2)=24, biCompression(4)=0 (BI_RGB, uncompressed), biSizeImage(4)=pixel_data_size, biXPelsPerMeter(4)=0, biYPelsPerMeter(4)=0, biClrUsed(4)=0, biClrImportant(4)=0
    info_header = struct.pack('<IIIHHIIIIII', 40, width, height, 1, 24, 0, pixel_data_size, 0, 0, 0, 0)
    # Pixel data: bottom row first, each pixel BGR, each row padded
    pixel_data = b""
    for y in reversed(range(height)):  # bottom-up: y=1 (bottom) first, then y=0 (top)
        row = pixels_top_to_bottom[y]
        row_bytes = b""
        for (r,g,b) in row:
            row_bytes += struct.pack('BBB', b,g,r)  # BGR
        # Pad to row_padded
        padding = row_padded - len(row_bytes)
        row_bytes += b"\x00"*padding
        pixel_data += row_bytes
    return file_header + info_header + pixel_data

# Test with same colors as test2x2.png: top-left red (255,0,0), top-right green (0,255,0), bottom-left blue (0,0,255), bottom-right white (255,255,255)

# `PIXterm` - *draw images in your ANSI terminal with true color*

**`PIXterm`** ***shows images directly in your terminal***, recreating the pixels through a combination of [ANSI character background color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code#Colors) and the [unicode lower half block element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_Elements). If image has transparency, an optional matte color can be used for background. Also, you can specify a dithering mode; in which case, the image is rendered using block elements with different shades, or using standard ASCII characters in the same way. In dithering mode, the matte color is used to fill the background of the blocks or characters.

Supported image formats: JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF, WebP.

Fetching images from HTTP/HTTPS is supported too.

## Usage

```
pixterm [options] <image file or URL>
</output>

import pty, os, subprocess, struct, fcntl, termios, select

def run_pty(args, rows, cols):
    master, slave = pty.openpty()
    winsize = struct.pack("HHHH", rows, cols, 0, 0)
    fcntl.ioctl(slave, termios.TIOCSWINSZ, winsize)
    proc = subprocess.Popen(['./executable']+args, stdout=slave, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, close_fds=True)

    _os.close(slave)
    output=b""

            data=_os.read(master, 65536)
            if not data:

            output+=data

func isHexDigit(c byte) bool {
	return (c >= '0' && c <= '9') || (c >= 'a' && c <= 'f') || (c >= 'A' && c <= 'F')
}
func hexVal(c byte) int {
	if c >= '0' && c <= '9' {
		return int(c - '0')
	}
	if c >= 'a' && c <= 'f' {
		return int(c-'a') + 10
	}
	return int(c-'A') + 10
}
func parseHexByte(s string) int {
	// s length 2, hex digits
	return hexVal(s[0])*16 + hexVal(s[1])
}

func parseMatte(s string) (r, g, b uint8, ok bool) {
	if s == "" {
		return 0, 0, 0, true
	}
	n := len(s)
	if n == 1 || n == 2 || n == 4 {
		return 0, 0, 0, false
	}
	if n == 3 {
		for i := 0; i < 3; i++ {
			if !isHexDigit(s[i]) {
				return 0, 0, 0, false
			}
		}
		rv := hexVal(s[0])*17
		gv := hexVal(s[1])*17
		bv := hexVal(s[2])*17
		return uint8(rv), uint8(gv), uint8(bv), true
	}
	// n >=5 or n==0 handled, n==1,2,4 already false. n==3 handled. So n>=5 (including 5,6,7,...)
	if n >= 5 {
		for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
			if !isHexDigit(s[i]) {
				return 0, 0, 0, false
			}
		}
		if n == 5 {
			rv := parseHexByte(s[0:2])
			gv := parseHexByte(s[2:4])
			bv := hexVal(s[4])
			return uint8(rv), uint8(gv), uint8(bv), true
		}
		// n>=6: check first 6 all hex?
		first6ok := true
		for i := 0; i < 6; i++ {
			if !isHexDigit(s[i]) {
				first6ok = false
				break
			}
		}
		if first6ok {
			rv := parseHexByte(s[0:2])
			gv := parseHexByte(s[2:4])
			bv := parseHexByte(s[4:6])
			return uint8(rv), uint8(gv), uint8(bv), true
		}
		// fallback to first 5 as 2+2+1 (since first 5 valid, index5 invalid)
		rv := parseHexByte(s[0:2])
		gv := parseHexByte(s[2:4])
		bv := hexVal(s[4])
		return uint8(rv), uint8(gv), uint8(bv), true
	}
	return 0, 0, 0, false
}

func isTTY() bool {
	fi, err := os.Stdout.Stat()
	if err != nil {
		return false
	}
	return (fi.Mode() & os.ModeCharDevice) != 0
}

type winsize struct {
	Row    uint16
	Col    uint16
	Xpixel uint16
	Ypixel uint16
}

func getWinsize() (rows, cols int, ok bool) {
	var ws winsize
	_, _, errno := syscall.Syscall(syscall.SYS_IOCTL, uintptr(syscall.Stdout), syscall.TIOCGWINSZ, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&ws)))
	if errno != 0 {
		return 0, 0, false
	}
	return int(ws.Row), int(ws.Col), true
}

func resizeLanczos(srcR, srcG, srcB []uint8, srcW, srcH, dstW, dstH int) (dstR, dstG, dstB []uint8) {
	// horizontal pass: srcH rows, each srcW -> dstW, with uint8 rounding intermediate
	interR := make([]uint8, dstW*srcH)
	interG := make([]uint8, dstW*srcH)
	interB := make([]uint8, dstW*srcH)
	for y := 0; y < srcH; y++ {
		rowR := make([]float64, srcW)
		rowG := make([]float64, srcW)
		rowB := make([]float64, srcW)
		for x := 0; x < srcW; x++ {
			idx := y*srcW + x
			rowR[x] = float64(srcR[idx])
			rowG[x] = float64(srcG[idx])
			rowB[x] = float64(srcB[idx])
		}
		scaledR := scale1DLanczos(rowR, dstW, 3)
		scaledG := scale1DLanczos(rowG, dstW, 3)
		scaledB := scale1DLanczos(rowB, dstW, 3)
		for x := 0; x < dstW; x++ {

			interR[idx] = clampRound(scaledR[x])
			interG[idx] = clampRound(scaledG[x])
			interB[idx] = clampRound(scaledB[x])
		}
	}
	// vertical pass: dstW cols, each srcH -> dstH
	dstR = make([]uint8, dstW*dstH)
	dstG = make([]uint8, dstW*dstH)

		colG := make([]float64, srcH)
		colB := make([]float64, srcH)

			colG[y] = float64(interG[idx])
			colB[y] = float64(interB[idx])

		scaledG := scale1DLanczos(colG, dstH, 3)
		scaledB := scale1DLanczos(colB, dstH, 3)
		for y := 0; y < dstH; y++ {

func buildImage(tr, tc, d, s int, mr, mg, mb uint8, img image.Image) (outR, outG, outB []uint8, outW, outH int, err error) {
	srcR, srcG, srcB, srcW, srcH := flattenWithMatte(img, mr, mg, mb)
	_ = d
	if s == 0 {
		dstW := tc
		dstH := tr*2 + 2
		scaledR, scaledG, scaledB := resizeLanczos(srcR, srcG, srcB, srcW, srcH, dstW, dstH)
		// top-crop drop top2 to get dstW x (dstH-2) = tc x tr*2
		outW = dstW
		outH = dstH - 2
		outR = make([]uint8, outW*outH)
		outG = make([]uint8, outW*outH)
		outB = make([]uint8, outW*outH)
		for y := 0; y < outH; y++ {
			for x := 0; x < outW; x++ {
				srcIdx := (y+2)*dstW + x
				dstIdx := y*outW + x
				outR[dstIdx] = scaledR[srcIdx]
				outG[dstIdx] = scaledG[srcIdx]
				outB[dstIdx] = scaledB[srcIdx]
			}
		}
		return outR, outG, outB, outW, outH, nil
	} else if s == 1 {
		dstW := tc
		dstH := tr*2 + 2
		scaleW := float64(dstW) / float64(srcW)
		scaleH := float64(dstH) / float64(srcH)
		scale := scaleW
		if scaleH > scale {
			scale = scaleH
		}
		scaledW := int(float64(srcW) * scale)
		scaledH := int(float64(srcH) * scale)
		if scaledW < 1 {
			scaledW = 1
		}
		if scaledH < 1 {
			scaledH = 1
		}
		scaledR, scaledG, scaledB := resizeLanczos(srcR, srcG, srcB, srcW, srcH, scaledW, scaledH)
		left := (scaledW - dstW) / 2
		top := (scaledH - dstH) / 2
		if left < 0 {
			left = 0
		}
		if top < 0 {
			top = 0
		}
		croppedR := make([]uint8, dstW*dstH)
		croppedG := make([]uint8, dstW*dstH)
		croppedB := make([]uint8, dstW*dstH)
		for y := 0; y < dstH; y++ {
			for x := 0; x < dstW; x++ {
				sx := left + x
				sy := top + y
				if sx < 0 {
					sx = 0
				}
				if sx >= scaledW {
					sx = scaledW - 1
				}
				if sy < 0 {
					sy = 0
				}
				if sy >= scaledH {
					sy = scaledH - 1
				}
				srcIdx := sy*scaledW + sx
				dstIdx := y*dstW + x
				croppedR[dstIdx] = scaledR[srcIdx]
				croppedG[dstIdx] = scaledG[srcIdx]
				croppedB[dstIdx] = scaledB[srcIdx]
			}
		}
		outW = dstW
		outH = dstH - 2
		outR = make([]uint8, outW*outH)
